name: The desired/desirable fallacy in J. S. Mill's proof of utilitarianism
plain_explanation: Mill argued that just as the only things visible are things people see, the only things desirable are things people desire -- but Russell points out 'visible' means 'able to be seen' while 'desirable' means 'ought to be desired,' so the analogy fails and the argument proves nothing.
precise_definition: Russell's logical critique of Mill's inference from 'pleasure is the only thing desired' to 'pleasure is the only thing desirable,' turning on the equivocation between a purely descriptive capacity-suffix ('-ible' as 'can be') and a normative one ('-ible' as 'ought to be').
why_it_mattered: It shows that Utilitarianism's central ethical claim cannot be derived from psychological facts about desire alone, a version of what is later called the naturalistic fallacy.
objections: Russell further argues that if each man must always pursue his own pleasure, saying he 'ought' to do otherwise is pointless, reducing ethics to mere prudence and politics to 'log-rolling'
